description: Branching scenario labs. Wrong choices show consequences and a hint before allowing retry, rather than a plain 'incorrect' mark. On correct completion, the badge name below must be added to the user's unlocked_badges array exactly as written (matches shared_data_schema.md convention, e.g. 'Quantum Novice', 'RSA Hacker').

scenarios.title: The Patient Records Leak
scenarios.setup: You're the security lead at a hospital. Your patient records are encrypted with RSA-2048 and must remain confidential for 25 years per regulation. An intelligence report indicates a foreign actor has been silently intercepting and storing your encrypted traffic for the past year.
scenarios.prompt: A threat actor has stolen your encrypted data today and will decrypt it in 5-10 years using a quantum computer. Which mitigation strategy do you apply?

choices.text: Do nothing — RSA-2048 hasn't been broken yet, so there's no current risk.
choices.feedback: Incorrect. This ignores 'Harvest Now, Decrypt Later.' Data with a 25-year confidentiality requirement is at risk today because it's already being captured.

choices.text: Begin migrating long-lifetime data flows to hybrid classical+PQC encryption (e.g., ECDHE + ML-KEM) immediately, prioritized by data sensitivity and lifetime.
choices.feedback: Correct. This directly addresses HNDL risk and hedges against any early flaws in newer PQC algorithms.

choices.text: Switch immediately to pure ML-KEM with no classical fallback, since PQC is 'quantum-safe.'
choices.feedback: Risky. Dropping classical crypto entirely removes the safety net if a bug is later found in a newly standardized algorithm — hybrid is the recommended transition strategy.

scenarios.title: The Cracked Chain of Trust
scenarios.setup: Your organization's root CA still signs certificates using RSA-2048. A Q-CAPS scan flags this as a long-term migration risk across 40 downstream systems.
scenarios.prompt: You have limited migration budget this quarter. What's the most crypto-agile first move?

choices.text: Re-issue all 40 downstream certificates individually with ML-DSA signatures, leaving the root CA unchanged.
choices.feedback: Inefficient and inconsistent. If the root CA stays RSA-based, the whole chain still depends on it — you'd need to redo this work later.

choices.text: Pilot a hybrid root CA (RSA + ML-DSA signatures) first, then cascade migration down the chain in priority order of asset criticality.
choices.feedback: Correct. Migrating the root first, in hybrid mode, protects the entire chain and follows crypto-agility best practice.

choices.text: Ignore the root CA and only patch the 5 lowest-criticality systems first, since they're 'easiest.'
choices.feedback: This misprioritizes effort — migration should follow risk and criticality, not ease of implementation.

scenarios.title: The Overlooked AES Key
scenarios.setup: A Q-CAPS scan of your file storage system shows AES-128 encryption protecting archived financial records with a 10-year retention requirement.
scenarios.prompt: Grover's algorithm roughly halves effective symmetric key strength against a quantum attacker. What should you do?

choices.text: Leave it as-is — AES-128 is still considered 'strong' classically.
choices.feedback: Incomplete. Its effective strength against a future quantum attacker (~64-bit equivalent) is inadequate for a 10-year retention requirement.

choices.text: Upgrade to AES-256 for all newly stored data with long retention, and prioritize re-encrypting the most sensitive existing archives.
choices.feedback: Correct. Doubling key length is a well-understood mitigation for Grover's algorithm's quadratic speedup.

choices.text: Switch to ML-KEM for the archived files instead of AES.
choices.feedback: Mismatched tool. ML-KEM is a key-exchange mechanism, not a symmetric encryption algorithm.

scenarios.title: The Spinning Coin Interview
scenarios.setup: During a mock technical interview, the interviewer asks you to explain, in one sentence a non-technical manager would understand, why a qubit isn't 'just a faster classical bit.'
scenarios.prompt: Which explanation correctly captures superposition without overclaiming what it means?

choices.text: "A qubit can be 0 and 1 at the same time, so quantum computers can try every answer simultaneously for free."
choices.feedback: Overclaims. Measurement collapses superposition to one classical outcome — you don't get 'every answer for free'; algorithms must be engineered so the correct answer becomes more likely to be observed.

choices.text: "A qubit holds a combination of 0 and 1 until measured, like a spinning coin — that's what lets certain carefully designed algorithms explore possibilities far more efficiently than a classical computer."
choices.feedback: Correct. This captures superposition accurately without the common 'free parallel computation' overclaim.

choices.text: "A qubit is just a bit that runs at a higher clock speed."
choices.feedback: Incorrect. This describes classical hardware speed, not the fundamentally different quantum mechanical behavior of superposition.

scenarios.title: The Migration Budget Meeting
scenarios.setup: Your organization has limited budget this year for quantum-readiness work. Leadership asks you to justify why RSA/ECC migration gets more urgency and funding than simply doubling AES key lengths everywhere.

choices.text: "They're equally urgent — Shor's and Grover's algorithms pose the same level of threat to both."
choices.feedback: Incorrect. Shor's algorithm gives an exponential speedup against RSA/ECC (full break), while Grover's gives only a quadratic speedup against AES (halved effective strength) — these are very different severity levels.

choices.text: "RSA/ECC face a full break via Shor's algorithm (exponential speedup), while AES only faces a weakening via Grover's algorithm (quadratic speedup, fixed by simply doubling key length) — so RSA/ECC migration to entirely new algorithms is the harder, more urgent problem."
choices.feedback: Correct. This distinguishes the severity and remediation complexity correctly, which is exactly the reasoning that should drive budget prioritization.

choices.text: "Neither is a real concern until a quantum computer capable of breaking RSA-2048 actually exists."
choices.feedback: Incorrect. This ignores Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later risk — migration must start well before the threat fully materializes, given how long enterprise migration takes.

scenarios.title: The Combiner Bug Report
scenarios.setup: A security researcher reports that your organization's hybrid TLS handshake (ECDHE + ML-KEM) might have a subtle weakness — not in either individual algorithm, but in how the two shared secrets are combined into the final session key.
scenarios.prompt: What is the technically correct response?

choices.text: "That's impossible — if both ECDHE and ML-KEM are individually secure, the combination must automatically be secure too."
choices.feedback: Incorrect. This is exactly the hybrid-mode weakness category covered in PQC Attack Surface training — an insecure combiner construction can undermine security even when both individual algorithms remain secure.

choices.text: "Treat this seriously — hybrid combiner constructions require their own dedicated security analysis, separate from validating each individual algorithm."
choices.feedback: Correct. Hybrid-mode weaknesses are a real, distinct attack surface category — combining two secure algorithms incorrectly can still introduce a new vulnerability.

choices.text: "Immediately drop ML-KEM and revert to classical-only ECDHE to eliminate the risk."
choices.feedback: Overcorrection. This abandons crypto-agility and PQC readiness rather than fixing the actual combiner issue — the correct move is analyzing and fixing the combiner, not abandoning the migration.

scenarios.title: The Boardroom Pitch
scenarios.setup: You have five minutes with the executive board to secure budget for a multi-year PQC migration. One board member says: "Quantum computers that can break encryption don't exist yet — why should we spend money on this now?"
scenarios.prompt: What is the single most effective response, per this program's risk framework?

choices.text: "You're right, let's revisit this in a few years once quantum computers are more advanced."
choices.feedback: Incorrect. This ignores Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later risk and the multi-year timeline real migrations require — waiting until the threat is imminent is too late.

choices.text: "The attack window opened the day our sensitive data was recorded, not the day the quantum computer arrives — and given how long enterprise migration takes, waiting means we're already behind."
choices.feedback: Correct. This is the exact framing from the program's risk management training — translating the technical HNDL concept into a business-urgency argument.

choices.text: "Every one of our systems is critically at risk right now and could be breached today."
choices.feedback: Overstates the case in a way that undermines credibility — the accurate claim is about future decryption risk on already-harvested data, not an active breach today.
